title: VTI vs. QQQ: Here's the ETF I'd Personally Buy and Hold for Decades
detail:
VTI vs. QQQ: Here's the ETF I'd Personally Buy and Hold for Decades
Ben Gran, The Motley Fool
Thu, October 29, 2026 at 7:50 AM EDT 5 min read
QQQ
^GSPC
Trade QQQ on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When it comes to investing, it's often said that "past performance does not guarantee future results." Just because a stock or exchange-traded fund (ETF) has performed well in the past doesn't mean it will be the best investment going forward. Investing is about the future. People constantly make decisions about where to put their money to work based on what they think will happen next, not what already happened.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index is a good example. It has been one of the best investments of the past 10 to 15 years. During the past 10 years, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ), an ETF that tracks the Nasdaq-100, has delivered an average annual total return of 20.5%. "The Qs" ETF has strongly outperformed the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) during that time.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Data by

YCharts.

The past performance of this Nasdaq-100 ETF has been phenomenal, right? Here's the thing: I'm concerned about future returns. When I consider new investments, I plan for the long run -- like 20 years or longer. I believe it's unlikely that U.S. tech stocks will maintain their recent track record of outperformance. There's another ETF that I like better than QQQ for the next few decades.

Let's look at why I'm investing in the Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (NYSEMKT: VTI) -- not QQQ -- for decades to come.

Image source: Getty Images.
Why buy VTI instead of QQQ? Slower growth for growth stocks

If you believe that today's biggest winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom are likely to keep winning for years to come, then you might want to buy the Invesco QQQ Trust. That tech ETF gives you a targeted way to own the biggest, most profitable tech companies.

But I'm not convinced that those 100 major tech names will be the best stocks to own for the next few decades. Recent Vanguard research projects that the ultimate winners of AI might not be today's AI stocks. As Vanguard's global head of capital market research, Qian Wang, said in a recent interview: "If AI truly transforms the economy, the ultimate winners may be the AI's end users that improve productivity without bearing the upfront investment."

In other words, it might not be the tech companies that are building AI tools today (and spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI data centers) that deliver the biggest stock market returns tomorrow. Instead, it might be smaller companies, value-stock companies, and less tech-intensive industries that win the most from AI. The best investments today might be stocks and sectors that have been overlooked or underpriced while most investors focused all their energy on tech.

The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady Wednesday, but two policymakers voted for another hike, highlighting concern over persistent inflation.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted 10–2 to maintain rates at 3.75%–4.00%, with Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both favoring a quarter-point increase.

It was Cook's first dissent since joining the Fed in 2022, coming as President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to remove her from office.

The Fed's statement described economic activity as expanding strongly, with resilient domestic spending and robust investment, despite continued geopolitical uncertainty.

"Inflation remains elevated," the committee said.

Polymarket Sees December Hike Odds Climb

On Polymarket, traders now assign an 82% probability to a 25-basis-point increase in December, up from roughly 77% before Wednesday's announcement.

The market has attracted more than $5.3 million in trading volume, with traders focused on whether Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will signal another increase before year-end.

Jesse Marre, senior portfolio manager at Hilbert Group, had expected the Fed to hold off until December rather than surprise markets with an immediate hike.

"I would be very surprised if the Fed shocked the market with a hike that is neither immediately required nor urgent when it can go in December instead," Marre said ahead of the announcement.

Inflation Pressures Persist Despite Weak Hiring.

Despite September's weak jobs report, which showed employers added just 29,000 positions, the Fed said job gains have kept pace with the workforce and unemployment has changed little.

Inflation-data provider Truflation forecasts September's Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation at 3.6% annually, up from 3.4% in August.

Its estimates show gasoline and other energy goods rising 33.7% year over year, amid surging oil prices and supply disruptions linked to the Iran war.

Last week's rising crude prices helped push the Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (NYSE:XLE) to a record high.

If oil remains elevated, it could strengthen the case for another rate hike in December, even with hiring weak.

The official PCE report arrives Thursday at 8:30 a.m. ET, alongside third-quarter GDP figures. Hotter-than-expected inflation or stronger economic growth could reinforce bets on a December hike, while softer data may ease pressure on the Fed.

That could have significant implications for the tech-heavy Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), as higher interest rates tend to weigh on growth-stock valuations.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Apple didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat AAPL. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

For four decades, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and the Nasdaq-100 mostly moved together. As reported on October 26, 2026, Apple's trailing three-month correlation with the index has fallen to about -0.1, per traders at Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS). That is the first negative reading on record, down from 0.91 in 2025.

24/7 Wall St.

Correlation measures how closely two assets move. A reading of one means they move in tandem, zero means there is no relationship, and a negative number means they tend to move in opposite directions. Our calculation uses 63 trading days of daily returns and puts the figure at -0.11 at the October 27 close, against both the index and the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ).

A reading like that stands out for a company that held about a 7.5% index weighting as of September. On October 27, both rose: Apple gained 0.93% to $347.10, and QQQ gained 1.27% to $721.25. The break shows up over weeks of trading, so a single day won't reveal it.

Record-Low Correlation Has Held Since August

In data going back to October 1985, the measure never fell below zero before August 2026. Its lowest earlier reading was +0.10 on October 18, 1996, and its peak was 0.97 on June 1, 2020 (our calculation).

Goldman's Rich Privorotsky flagged the largest tech selling ever in Goldman's prime brokerage book, citing rising capital costs and AI overcrowding.

S&P 500, growth, and target-date funds all concentrate in the same mega-cap names, meaning a "diversified" 401(k) can carry 40% exposure to one AI trade.

A 25% drop in that concentrated slice costs a $900,000 saver roughly $90,000, and at 63 that kind of forced selling turns paper losses into permanent ones.

The biggest 401k decisions tend to get made once and never revisited: when to roll it over, what to hold inside it, and when to start taking money out. That is exactly what the report: 401k & IRA Tips and Answers was created to address, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Picture a 63-year-old with $900,000 in her 401(k), divided among an S&P 500 index fund, a growth fund and a target-date fund. She figures three funds mean three different sources of risk. Her situation is hypothetical, but the assumption is familiar.

DC Studio / Shutterstock.com

Goldman Sachs just gave her a reason to check. On the firm's The Markets podcast, recorded Oct. 22 and posted Oct. 23, Rich Privorotsky, head of European Equities Trading in Goldman's FICC and Equities division, said investors were de-risking out of a crowded trade in AI, semiconductor and hyperscaler stocks. He cited rising capital costs, power constraints and more competition. He also said the prior week saw the largest tech selling ever recorded in Goldman's prime brokerage book.

The pressure is showing up in stock prices. Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down about 4% over the past month and still up about 16% this year. Privorotsky called hyperscaler earnings the key test, and those reports land alongside a Fed decision in a crucial two-week stretch for stocks.

Three Funds Sharing One Set of Top Holdings

Index funds weight companies by market value, so the largest companies take the largest slices. Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA:VOO) had 38% of its assets in information technology at midyear.
